purpose: Benralizumab is used to help control severe asthma in adults and children (12 and older) whose asthma is not well managed with their usual inhalers. It works best for people whose asthma is driven by high levels of a certain type of white blood cell called eosinophils. It can reduce asthma attacks and may allow some patients to take less oral steroid medication.
how_it_works: Your body has white blood cells called eosinophils that, in some people, cause airway swelling and trigger asthma attacks. Benralizumab is a special protein (called a monoclonal antibody) that attaches to those eosinophils and signals your immune system to destroy them. By greatly reducing eosinophil levels, the drug helps calm the inflammation in your airways so you breathe more easily.
common_side_effects: Headache, sore throat, and reactions at the injection site such as redness, pain, or swelling are the most common side effects. Some people may also feel mild fever or tiredness after their injection.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have any current infections before starting this medication, as benralizumab can affect your immune system. Do not use it to treat a sudden asthma attack — it is not a rescue medication. Rarely, some people have serious allergic reactions (anaphylaxis) usually within hours of the injection, so your first few doses may be given in a clinic where staff can watch you. Also tell your doctor about any parasitic (worm-type) infections, as eosinophils help fight those.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is one injection (30 mg under the skin) once every 4 weeks for the first 3 doses, and then once every 8 weeks after that. It is given as a shot under the skin of the upper arm, thigh, or belly. After proper training, some patients can give themselves the injection at home using an autoinjector pen.
